abstract: Previous studies suggested that early visual deprivation results in global motion processing deficits. These deficits were typically attributed to poor integration of local motion signals. We challenge this view by dissociating motion integration from feature-based attentional selection. We tested 34 Ethiopian children who had bilateral congenital cataracts and gained pattern vision only years later. Strikingly, they were no different than their typically developing peers when the task required integration across motion directions, with performance well captured by a population vector-averaging model. Thus, core integration mechanisms remain intact despite prolonged early visual deprivation. In contrast, the same individuals were poorer than controls in the motion-coherence task requiring identification of a dominant motion direction. This dissociation is well explained by adding to the model a physiologically plausible attention-dependent process, which selectively amplifies salient motion signals via top-down feedback. Accordingly, the late sighted were impaired across other attention-demanding tasks. We therefore suggest that early visual deprivation disrupts attentional selection, not motion integration.
